concepts.definition: A personality construct describing whether individuals believe outcomes are controlled by internal actions (internal locus) or external forces (external locus); foundational for understanding perceived agency and personal causality beliefs.
key_refs: Rotter 1966 / Locus of Control Theory In Psychology
concepts.implication: MetroGraph must support internal locus of control through transparent action-outcome mappings; users should experience their explicit choices (clicking, filtering, querying) as directly causing graph changes, not system-mediated consequences.

concepts.definition: Bandura's concept of belief in one's capacity to execute actions and produce desired outcomes; foundational psychological theory underlying perceived control, agency, and motivation in technology use.
key_refs: Bandura 1997 / Self-Efficacy: The Exercise of Control
concepts.implication: MetroGraph's interaction design must enable mastery experiences through progressive complexity disclosure and clear success feedback; users should feel their learning and effort produce competence in graph querying and exploration.

concepts.definition: Optimal psychological state achieved through balance of challenge and skill, clear goals, immediate feedback, and sense of control; flow state is intrinsically motivated and characterized by loss of self-consciousness and time distortion.
key_refs: Csikszentmihalyi 1990 / Flow: The Psychology of Optimal Experience
concepts.implication: MetroGraph should calibrate graph complexity and task difficulty to user skill level; provide real-time feedback on queries, enable progressive disclosure of advanced features, and ensure immediate visibility of query results to sustain flow.

concepts.definition: Subjective experience of controlling one's body and external environment; comprises implicit pre-reflective feeling of agency and explicit judgement of agency; arises from integration of internal sensorimotor signals and external situational cues.
key_refs: Limerick, Coyle, Moore 2014 / The experience of agency in human-computer interactions
Limerick, Coyle, Moore 2022 / The sense of agency in emerging technologies
concepts.implication: MetroGraph must minimize latency, provide immediate system feedback to user actions (graph updates, highlights), and ensure predictability of cause-effect relationships in graph interactions to sustain sense of agency.

concepts.definition: Foundational HCI principle establishing that user interfaces should enable continuous visibility of objects, physical actions on them, and rapid reversible feedback; minimizes cognitive distance between intention and system response.
key_refs: Shneiderman 1983 / Direct Manipulation: A Fundamental Element of Graphical User Interfaces
concepts.implication: MetroGraph's graph nodes should be directly draggable, visually persistent, and immediately responsive to interaction; support undo/redo for reversibility; avoid modal dialogs that interrupt direct manipulation of graph elements.

concepts.definition: Perceptual qualities of objects that communicate possible actions; afford certain uses by their design; bridge the gulf of execution between user intention and system capabilities.
key_refs: Norman 2013 / The Design of Everyday Things (Revised)
Norman 2004 / Emotional Design
concepts.implication: MetroGraph nodes and edges should have clear visual affordances indicating interactivity (hover states, color encoding); use size, position, and color to afford filtering, grouping, and expansion operations without explicit labels.

concepts.definition: System signals communicated to users about action outcomes; enables users to perceive control and adjust future actions; critical for sense of agency and flow state maintenance.
key_refs: Shneiderman 1983
Limerick et al. 2014
Vig et al. 2022 / Sense of Agency and User Experience
concepts.implication: MetroGraph must provide sub-100ms feedback to user interactions (node selection, edge traversal); visual feedback should clearly indicate query state (pending, executing, complete) and match user mental models.

concepts.definition: Shneiderman's interface design rule mandating support for internal locus of control; users should feel they are in charge of the system and that systems respond to their actions, not system-mediated decisions.
key_refs: Shneiderman & Plaisant 2004 / Rules of Interface Design
Shneiderman 2022 / Human-Centered AI
concepts.implication: MetroGraph must make all graph transformations traceable to user actions; avoid silent algorithmic simplification or node collapsing without explicit user request; every graph change should be attributable to a user command.

concepts.definition: Theory that human action is fundamentally contextual and opportunistic rather than following pre-specified plans; emphasizes how agents respond to real-time environmental cues and situated constraints.
key_refs: Suchman 1987 / Plans and Situated Actions
concepts.implication: MetroGraph should support exploratory, non-linear graph navigation; avoid prescriptive query workflows; enable users to adjust exploration strategy on-the-fly based on emerging graph patterns rather than committing to pre-planned analysis.

concepts.definition: Theory modeling user agency in information-seeking as adaptive behavior driven by information scent; users evaluate patches and diet based on cost-benefit tradeoffs, pursuing high-scent trails and abandoning low-scent ones.
key_refs: Pirolli & Card 1999 / Information Foraging Theory
concepts.implication: MetroGraph must provide strong information scent through visual encoding (node size, color saturation) showing result density and query relevance; enable rapid scent evaluation to support user agency in deciding which graph paths to explore.

concepts.definition: Internal representations users construct of how systems work; mismatches between user mental models and system behavior cause confusion and errors; shared mental models enable effective collaboration.
key_refs: Norman 2013 / The Design of Everyday Things
Norman on Mental Models
concepts.implication: MetroGraph's visual metaphor (metro map style) should match users' spatial/network mental models; consistent edge labels, node attributes, and interaction patterns enable users to predict system behavior and exercise agency confidently.

concepts.definition: Shneiderman's 2D framework separating automation level (none to full) from human control level (none to full); advocates for high-automation, high-control designs where AI augments rather than replaces human judgment.
key_refs: Shneiderman 2022 / Human-Centered AI: Ensuring Human Control While Increasing Automation
concepts.implication: MetroGraph should enable high automation (intelligent suggestions, pattern detection) paired with high user control (override mechanism, transparency about AI recommendations); position graph suggestions as aids, not directives.

concepts.definition: Technical and procedural capacity for humans to understand, monitor, and override autonomous system decisions; requires transparency mechanisms, predictable system behavior, and accessible override options.
key_refs: Rahwan 2025 / Human-controllable AI: Meaningful Human Control
concepts.implication: MetroGraph's algorithmic graph simplification, recommendation ranking, or layout must be explainable; users must be able to disable/override suggestions and understand the criteria driving system recommendations.

concepts.definition: Visibility of system decision-making processes, data sources, and algorithmic criteria; enables users to evaluate AI outputs, build appropriate trust, and exercise informed control over system behavior.
key_refs: Wang et al. 2026 / Seeing to Think? How Source Transparency Design Shapes Interactive Information Seeking
Yang 2024 / From Explainable to Interactive AI
concepts.implication: MetroGraph should surface the data sources and query logic underlying graph suggestions; show why certain nodes/edges appear, what fields were filtered, enabling users to understand and critique system outputs.

concepts.definition: Human tendency to over-rely on automated systems and under-weight contradictory evidence from non-automated sources; compromises user agency through reduced critical evaluation of system outputs.
key_refs: Wickens 2015 / Human-Automation Interaction Research: Past, Present, and Future
concepts.implication: MetroGraph should avoid presenting algorithmic recommendations without qualification; always show confidence levels, alternative suggestions, and mechanisms for user challenge/override to maintain critical stance.

concepts.definition: Systems enabling dynamic, task-dependent allocation of control between human and AI; humans and systems take turns initiating actions based on situation context; preserves user agency while leveraging automation.
key_refs: Horvitz 1999 / Mixed-Initiative Context
concepts.implication: MetroGraph should enable users to initiate exploration then accept system suggestions, or reject suggestions and take manual control; control allocation should be transparent (clear who is in charge at any moment).

concepts.definition: Bidirectional influence between humans and autonomous systems; control is negotiated rather than fixed; systems influence human choices while respecting human authority and values.
key_refs: Taddeo 2024 / Negotiating the Shared Agency between Humans & AI in the Recommender System
Lim 2026 / When to Hand Off, When to Work Together
Mohseni 2024 / Complementarity in Human-AI Collaboration
concepts.implication: MetroGraph must make explicit when users are responding to system suggestions vs. acting independently; support users teaching the system about their preferences through feedback mechanisms (marking results as relevant/irrelevant).

concepts.definition: Nissenbaum's framework for privacy grounded in norms of appropriate information flow within contexts; privacy violations occur when information moves to inappropriate contexts; enables user control over data flows.
key_refs: Nissenbaum 2009 / Values in Design
Nissenbaum / Regulatory CI: Adaptively Regulating Privacy as Contextual Integrity
concepts.implication: MetroGraph should clarify data usage contexts and enable users to control what metadata (query history, exploration patterns) is retained or shared; make explicit the norms governing data access and retention.

concepts.definition: HCI methodology systematically integrating human values (autonomy, privacy, informed consent, fairness) into design through conceptual, empirical, and technical investigations; treats values as design constraints.
key_refs: Friedman & Hendry 2003 / Value Sensitive Design and Information Systems
concepts.implication: MetroGraph should be designed with explicit value commitments to user autonomy (explicit control), transparency (clear mechanics), and fairness (no hidden algorithmic manipulation); conduct empirical studies validating these values are supported.

concepts.definition: Recommendation mechanisms that preserve user agency through explicit control levers enabling users to adjust exploration strategy, filter diversity, and resist algorithmic filter bubbles.
key_refs: Kirman 2022 / User-controllable Recommendation Against Filter Bubbles
Xie 2025 / Design of a Serendipity-Incorporated Recommender System
concepts.implication: MetroGraph recommendations (e.g., suggested nodes, paths, patterns) should include user-adjustable controls: diversity slider, confidence threshold, recommendation style toggle; make serendipity an explicit option.

concepts.definition: Taxonomy of distinct collaborative modes between humans and AI ranging from simple (system-initiated, one-way recommendations) to complex (reciprocal turn-taking, multi-step dialogue); empirical review reveals dominance of simplistic patterns.
key_refs: Liu et al. 2024 / Human-AI collaboration is not very collaborative yet
concepts.implication: MetroGraph should go beyond simple recommendations to support reciprocal interaction patterns; enable users to ask follow-up questions about suggestions, critique results, and dynamically adjust query strategy in conversation-like flow.

concepts.concept: Sense of Agency & User Experience Relationship
concepts.definition: Empirical relationship between users' perceived sense of agency and overall satisfaction/UX; system feedback mechanisms and control responsiveness significantly impact both agency and user satisfaction.
key_refs: Vig et al. 2022 / Sense of Agency and User Experience: Is There a Link?
concepts.implication: MetroGraph's success depends on supporting sense of agency; every design decision about responsiveness, feedback visibility, and control transparency directly impacts user satisfaction and adoption.

concepts.definition: Shared understanding of AI system state, capabilities, and current actions enabling human operators to maintain predictability and agency; requires transparency about agent behavior and intentions.
key_refs: Goler 2023 / Agent Teaming Situation Awareness (ATSA)
Degani 2016 / Human Factors Considerations in Aviation
concepts.implication: MetroGraph should clearly display algorithmic system state (what suggestions are being computed, what data is being accessed); enable users to interrupt/pause automated processes and understand what the system is doing at any moment.

concepts.definition: Tension between automated personalization/adaptation and user autonomy; adaptive systems must provide transparency and override mechanisms to preserve user sense of control when systems adjust behavior.
key_refs: Scheuerman 2014 / User Control in Adaptive User Interfaces for Accessibility
Amershi 2025 / Autonomy Reshapes How Personalization Affects Privacy Concerns
concepts.implication: MetroGraph should support personalization (remembering user preferences) but make personalizations visible and modifiable; users should understand why the interface adapted and be able to reset to defaults.

concepts.definition: User perception of fairness in algorithmic outcomes influenced by transparency, development procedures, and understanding; users perceive algorithms as fairer when they understand decision criteria.
key_refs: Anjomshoae 2019 / Factors Influencing Perceived Fairness in Algorithmic Decision-Making
concepts.implication: MetroGraph's graph algorithms (ranking, layout, clustering) should be explainable; show criteria and trade-offs (e.g., why certain nodes are grouped, why edges are weighted); users perceive fairer outcomes when decisions are transparent.
